channel.title: How Biscuit
channel.description: Practical, evidence-aware guides for technology, home, kitchens, shopping decisions, and useful tools.

item.title: Why Is My Dehumidifier Running but Not Collecting Water?
item.description: A dehumidifier may stop collecting because the room is already below the setpoint, the room is too cold, airflow is blocked, the bucket or drain is wrong, or the compressor has failed.

item.title: Dehumidifier vs. Air Conditioner: Which Do You Need?
item.description: An air conditioner removes heat and some moisture. A dehumidifier removes moisture but returns heat to the room. Choose from temperature, humidity, moisture source, and room conditions.

item.title: Home Humidity and Dehumidifier Checklist
item.description: Measure humidity room by room, find moisture sources, choose dehumidifier capacity, check drainage and safety, and download the printable three-day room log.

item.title: How Much Does a Dehumidifier Cost to Run?
item.description: Calculate dehumidifier cost from watts, runtime, measured kWh, or annual certified energy use. A 500-watt full-power example costs about 9 cents per hour at 18.44 cents/kWh.

item.title: What Humidity Should Your House Be?
item.description: Keep indoor relative humidity around 30% to 50% when practical and below 60%. Learn how seasons, condensation, basements, leaks, and measurement affect the right target.

item.title: What Size Dehumidifier Do You Need?
item.description: Choose dehumidifier capacity from the space size and how damp it is. ENERGY STAR recommends 20-30 pints for many damp rooms under 2,000 square feet and more for wetter or larger spaces.

item.title: Air Fryer vs. Oven Electricity Cost
item.description: Compare exact wattage, preheat, cooking time, batches, and servings. A small air fryer often uses less for a small meal, but capacity can reverse the result.

item.title: Can a Microwave Interfere With Wi-Fi?
item.description: A microwave oven can interfere with nearby 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi while it is running. Test the pattern, move equipment, or use 5 GHz or 6 GHz where supported.

item.title: Download Speed vs. Upload Speed vs. Latency
item.description: Download speed moves data to you, upload moves it away, and latency measures delay. Learn which metric affects streaming, calls, backups, gaming, and remote work.

item.title: Ethernet vs. Wi-Fi: Which Is Faster and More Reliable?
item.description: Ethernet is usually more consistent and avoids wireless interference, but its real speed is limited by the slowest port, adapter, cable, switch, router, or internet connection.

item.title: How Much Does a Dishwasher Cost Per Load?
item.description: Divide annual kWh by annual test cycles, then multiply by your rate. A 240 kWh/year dishwasher works out to about 21 cents per standardized cycle at 18.44 cents/kWh.

item.title: How Much Does an Electric Dryer Cost Per Load?
item.description: Estimate dryer cost from measured or certified kWh per cycle. A standardized electric-dryer example can range from about 17 to 40 cents per test load at 18.44 cents/kWh.

item.title: How Much Does an Electric Oven Cost Per Hour?
item.description: Multiply oven kilowatts by active hours and your electric rate, but account for preheat and thermostat cycling. A 3,000-watt full-power example costs 55 cents per hour at 18.44 cents/kWh.

item.title: How Much Does a Refrigerator Cost to Run?
item.description: Multiply the refrigerator's EnergyGuide annual kWh by your local electricity rate. A 400 kWh/year example costs about $6.15 per month at 18.44 cents/kWh.

item.title: How Much Internet Speed Do You Need?
item.description: Add the official bandwidth needs of simultaneous streams and calls, then account for upload, latency, Wi-Fi, and variation. Use this household planning guide.

item.title: How Often Should You Replace Your Wi-Fi Router?
item.description: There is no universal router lifespan. Replace it when support ends, security is obsolete, failures persist, or the hardware cannot meet verified household needs.

item.title: How to Calculate What an Appliance Costs to Run
item.description: Calculate appliance cost from annual kWh, measured kWh, or watts and time. Learn which method works for refrigerators, dryers, dishwashers, ovens, and small appliances.

item.title: Mesh Wi-Fi vs. Range Extender: Which Should You Use?
item.description: Use a range extender for one isolated weak area and mesh for broader multi-room coverage, but diagnose placement, backhaul, compatibility, and router support first.

item.title: Does Aluminum Foil Improve Wi-Fi Signal?
item.description: Metal can redirect Wi-Fi, but the famous study used computer-optimized 3D reflectors coated with foil. Random kitchen foil can help one direction and hurt another.

item.title: How Much Does a Washing Machine Cost Per Load?
item.description: Divide the washer's annual EnergyGuide kWh by your actual yearly loads, then multiply by your electric rate. Learn how water temperature and drying change the real cost.

item.title: How Much Electricity Does a Microwave Use?
item.description: Multiply the microwave's electrical input watts by cooking time and your electric rate. A 1,500-watt input example costs about 5 cents for 10 minutes.

item.title: Where Should You Place a Wi-Fi Extender?
item.description: Put the extender roughly halfway between the router and weak area, but only where it still receives a strong upstream signal. Test the link before moving farther.

item.title: Can You Refreeze Food After a Power Outage?
item.description: You can refreeze food that still contains ice crystals or remains at 40°F or below. Discard perishables held above 40°F for more than two hours.

item.title: Do You Need a Refrigerator Thermometer? What to Look For
item.description: Keep one appliance thermometer in the refrigerator and one in the freezer. Learn what type to buy, where to place it, and how to read it.

item.title: How Long Is Food Safe in the Refrigerator Without Power?
item.description: An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours during an outage. After that, move perishables to ice at 40°F or below or discard them.

item.title: How Long Will Food Stay Frozen During a Power Outage?
item.description: A full unopened freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours; a half-full freezer for about 24 hours. Check temperature and ice crystals afterward.

item.title: Power Outage Food Safety Chart: What to Keep and What to Throw Away
item.description: Use this refrigerator and freezer decision chart after an outage. It includes the four-hour, 48-hour, 24-hour, 40°F, and ice-crystal rules.

item.title: What Food Should You Throw Away After a Power Outage?
item.description: Discard refrigerated meat, milk, eggs, soft cheese, leftovers, and other perishables after four hours without safe cooling. Use this item-by-item guide.

item.title: Why Is My Electric Bill So High in Summer?
item.description: A high summer electric bill usually comes from more cooling hours, higher rates, a longer billing period, air leaks, or an inefficient system. Here is how to identify the cause.

item.title: How Much Does a Window AC Cost per Hour?
item.description: Calculate a window air conditioner’s hourly, daily, and monthly electricity cost from its wattage and your local electric rate.

item.title: 2.4 GHz vs. 5 GHz Wi-Fi: Which Should You Use?
item.description: Use 2.4 GHz when range and wall penetration matter; use 5 GHz when a nearby device needs more capacity. Learn why the router may choose automatically.

item.title: Best Place to Put Your Wi-Fi Router
item.description: Put your router near the center of the area you use, out in the open, off the floor, and away from dense barriers. Use this test before buying an extender.

item.title: Fan vs. Air Conditioner Cost: How Much Cheaper Is a Fan?
item.description: A fan usually costs far less to run than an air conditioner, but it does not lower room temperature. Compare hourly costs and learn when to use each.

item.title: How to Fix Wi-Fi Dead Zones Without Buying Anything
item.description: Map the weak area, move and raise the router, try another band, reduce interference, and test one change at a time before buying mesh or an extender.

item.title: Home Wi-Fi Dead-Zone Checklist
item.description: Record Wi-Fi performance room by room, test one change at a time, and decide whether the problem is your device, router placement, or internet service.

item.title: Why Does My Wi-Fi Keep Disconnecting?
item.description: Repeated Wi-Fi drops can come from weak signal, one problem device, modem trouble, power saving, saved settings, or router faults. Diagnose them in this order.

item.title: Why Is My Wi-Fi So Slow? 12 Things to Check Before Buying Anything
item.description: Slow Wi-Fi can come from weak signal, ISP trouble, congestion, router placement, or one problem device. Use this step-by-step diagnosis before buying new hardware.

item.title: How Much Does a Portable AC Cost to Run?
item.description: Calculate a portable air conditioner’s hourly and monthly electricity cost using its watts, runtime, and your local electricity rate.

item.title: Does Turning the AC Off Save Money?
item.description: Turning off or raising the AC when no one is home usually saves energy, but heat, humidity, pets, and health needs determine whether “off” is sensible.

item.title: Home Energy Check for a High Summer Electric Bill
item.description: Use this step-by-step home energy checklist to find why a summer electric bill increased, from billing days and rates to AC filters, air leaks, and hidden loads.

item.title: Why Salt Melts Ice (and When It Stops Working)
item.description: A plain-English field guide to freezing-point depression, brine, the limits of rock salt, and the least-wasteful way to de-ice a walk.

item.title: How Does Baking Powder Work?
item.description: Baking powder makes batter and dough rise by producing carbon dioxide bubbles. Here is what triggers it, what goes wrong, and how to test your can.

item.title: Why Are Some Answers Better Than Others?
item.description: A useful answer addresses the real question, explains its reasoning, shows the next move, and makes the limits of its evidence visible.
